title: Pastoral Counseling and Knowing When to Refer
subtitle: Soul care, the limits of the pastor's office, mental health, and the wisdom to send someone to a licensed counselor before harm is done

sections.title: The Office and the Table
sections.body:
Someone sits across from you at a counseling table and tells you something they have never told another soul. That is a sacred trust, and it is also a weight, and the two things arrive together.

A pastor is not a therapist. A pastor is something older and something narrower. You are a shepherd of souls, not a clinician of minds.

This distinction is not a demotion. It is the boundary that keeps you useful and keeps people safe. You bring Scripture, prayer, the long view of a person's life before God, the patient presence of someone who will still be there next year. You bring the church around them. What you do not bring is a license, a diagnosis, or the training to treat an illness. The moment you forget which table you sit at is the moment you start doing harm in the name of help.

sections.title: What the Pastor Can Actually Do
sections.body:
Do not undersell the office either. There is real soul care that only a pastor is positioned to give, and the rush to refer everything is its own failure.

You can name sin without condemning the sinner. You can speak forgiveness with authority. You can sit in grief without trying to cure it.

Most of what walks into a pastor's study is not a clinical disorder. It is a marriage going cold, a man crushed by guilt, a woman who cannot believe God could love her, a family in conflict, a believer in a long spiritual drought. These are the ordinary aches of being human in a fallen world, and they are exactly what the ministry of the Word and prayer and presence is built to address. So listen long before you speak. Ask more than you answer. Point steadily to Christ without using him as a way to end the conversation early. A great deal of healing happens at that table, slowly, the way most real healing happens.

sections.title: The Line You Must Not Cross
sections.body:
There is a line, and crossing it has wrecked people. You must learn to see it before you reach it.

When the suffering in front of you is not mainly spiritual but medical, you are out of your depth, and pretending otherwise is not faith. It is pride.

Depression that will not lift. Anxiety that has seized the body. Trauma that replays without ceasing. Addiction with its own physical grip. Thoughts of suicide, ever, in any form. An eating disorder. A mind losing contact with reality. These are illnesses, as real as a broken bone, and a Bible verse is not the treatment for a broken bone. The most spiritual thing you can do in these cases is say, plainly, this is beyond what I can help with, and I love you too much to pretend it is not. There is no shame in a doctor and there is no shame in a counselor. There is great shame in a shepherd who watches a sheep bleed out because he wanted to handle it himself.

sections.title: How to Refer Without Abandoning
sections.body:
Referral done badly feels like rejection. Done well, it feels like being handed up to better help by someone who is not letting go.

Do not say I cannot help you and close the door. Say I am going to make sure you get the right help, and I am still your pastor through all of it.

Keep a real list. Know the licensed counselors in your area, the ones who will not undermine a person's faith and the ones who simply do good clinical work. Know the doctors. Know the crisis line number by heart, because you will need it some night when there is no time to look it up. Then make the handoff warm. Help them make the call if making calls is part of what is hard for them. Walk with them to the first appointment if that is what it takes. And stay. Referral is not the end of your care. It is the addition of care you cannot provide. The counselor treats the illness. You keep tending the soul. The two of you are on the same side, and the person between you should feel held by both.

sections.title: The Counselor's Own Soul
sections.body:
You cannot give from a well that has run dry, and the pastor who counsels all week is often the one most starved for counsel himself.

The man who carries everyone's secrets is the man most tempted to carry his own alone. That is how shepherds quietly come apart.

So guard yourself. Have your own counselor or spiritual director, someone outside your congregation who knows what you are carrying. Learn the difference between a hard week and a soul in genuine trouble, in yourself as quickly as in others. Watch your own marriage, your own anger, your own creeping numbness. The forbidden secret of this work is how often the helper needs help and is too proud or too tired to get it. I have sat with people in their darkest hour and driven home to a darkness of my own I would not name. That is not strength. It is the beginning of the kind of collapse that ends ministries and wounds families. Take the same medicine you prescribe. A whole shepherd can keep sending the sheep to where the healing is. A broken one cannot even find it for himself.
